text: The war Johan is running from is being fought on another continent, and the drought he is driving through has no interest in it. Northeastern Brazil, 1942: a man selling aspirin along the back roads to stay clear of the German draft takes on a passenger, Ranulpho, who wants out of the dry country by whatever means present themselves. After that it is two men in a cab and a landscape going past, which puts the weight on distance, delay, and the awkwardness of sharing a vehicle with someone whose reasons cannot be shared. Marcelo Gomes runs it 99 minutes and keeps the war offscreen, a pressure on one man's itinerary and nothing whatever to the other. Brazil sent it to the Academy Awards, and the Abraccine survey of the hundred best Brazilian films kept it.

Uruguay is the entire plan, and it costs money that nobody in this group has. They ride with a taxi driver and rob the passengers he collects, until the size of their share starts to look like a robbery committed against them; working alone turns out to require competence none of them has acquired. The Silver Condor for best film went to it, a formal honour for a picture that stays at street level throughout — small takes, bad planning, a pregnancy setting a deadline that cannot be renegotiated. Bruno Stagnaro gives it ninety-two minutes and lets nobody rise. What gets measured, scene by scene, is the gap between what a day of work pays and what leaving the country costs. The destination never changes and never gets nearer.

The accident is staged; everything that has to be proved afterwards is real. Two men employed by a demolition company decide that their employer's corruption is a resource, and arrange an injury the firm can be made to pay for. What follows is a thriller in which the danger is largely administrative: a story that has to survive examination by people paid to take it apart, and a lie that holds only as long as it is never once relaxed, in public or otherwise. Adolfo Aristarain gives it 112 minutes and keeps most of the violence potential, which is harder to sustain than the alternative and much harder to walk away from. Argentina awarded it the Silver Condor for best film, and the surveys its film world takes of itself have gone on returning to it.

People were taken from their homes in Quebec in October 1970 and held for weeks while no charge was ever brought. Michel Brault made this four years afterwards out of what happened to some of them, and the governing decision is one of scale: not the crisis, not its politics, but the interval between a door opening and a person being released. The citizens are ordinary by design, since nothing about them accounts for their selection, and the method is to keep exact pace with a process that nobody involved will explain. It runs 109 minutes in French. Canada submitted it to the Academy Awards, it took the national award for best motion picture, and TIFF later set it among the ten Canadian films it holds highest.

An eleven-year-old orphan with a small criminal record gets seventy-nine minutes of undivided attention here, and no adult arrives to explain him. Argentina in 1965 is present as climate rather than as argument: authority is a condition of the boy's day, applied by people who have other things on. Leonardo Favio stays at the level of routine — waiting, repetition, hours that have to be filled — and lets the ordinary accumulate until it reads as a sentence being served. The brevity does real work: at this length nothing can be prepared for and no lesson has room to form. The Silver Condor for best film went to it and the Museo del Cine survey of Argentine cinema has kept it, though what it leaves behind is smaller than any list — the untheatrical duration of a child's afternoon.

A 136-minute film about a boxer cannot be made out of the fights; the arithmetic alone puts most of it outside the ring. Jose Maria Gatica was the leading figure in Argentine boxing through the 1940s and into the decade after, and the whole country called him el Mono, which is a fact about possession before it is a fact about sport. Leonardo Favio spends the running time on everything a highlight reel discards. A life lived that publicly is recorded mostly by other people, and working out which part of the record was ever the man's own is the problem any film about him inherits. Spain gave it the Goya for best Ibero-American film, Argentina submitted it to the Academy Awards, and a Silver Condor followed at home.

The Argentine western has no desert and no frontier town; it has grazing country, and the man who owns the ground is generally the man who enforces the law. Juan Moreira drives mules in the late nineteenth century and is good at the work, which protects him from nothing: police and landholders treat humiliation as routine equipment, used on people with no procedure for objecting. Leonardo Favio filmed it in 1973 at ninety-nine minutes, room enough for one man, a sequence of injuries, and the recognition that not one of them is personal. History, drama and western are all listed against it, and none of the three competes with the others; the period supplies the grievance, the genre supplies only the open ground.

Being loved is what goes wrong here: Aniceto had his solitude organised and functioning, and Francisca's offer is what exposes him. Sixty-three minutes is an odd length for a romance, and the shortness is the argument — no subplot to retreat into, no second couple, nothing standing between a man's limitations and the moment they surface. Leonardo Favio keeps the courtship, the work and the ordinary week at the size of two lives, small enough that meanness has nowhere to go and generosity gets no witnesses. The Silver Condor for best film went to it, a formal honour for something built at this scale, and the Museo del Cine survey has held on to it since. The original title, in Spanish, is longer than the plot.

Two brothers named Peralta go up the Alto Paraná for work, and the terms on arrival are nothing like the terms they were offered. Hugo del Carril made this in 1952, and its subject is procurement: how labour is recruited, moved, housed and used in a place far enough from anywhere that the employer's word is the only law on offer. The genre index says western, which fits in that the country is remote and the authority is private, and misleads in that nobody here is at liberty to ride away. Eighty-two minutes, most of them work. What carries it is the plainness of the accusation — the conditions are not the background of the story, they are the story. Argentina gave it the Silver Condor for best film, and it has stayed in the survey the Museo del Cine takes of the national cinema.

The source is a Broadway musical and the genre listing says horror; both are accurate. Benjamin Barker returns to London under the name Sweeney Todd, opens a barber's shop, and enters an arrangement with the woman he shares the building with, Mrs. Lovett, whose interests turn out to run alongside his own. Tim Burton takes the songs straight rather than sending them up, and across 116 minutes the numbers keep their theatrical shape while what they describe goes precisely where the second genre label promises. A razor is a working tool and a shop is a place of business; the film is unusually literal about both. It won the Golden Globe for best musical or comedy and a National Board of Review top-ten place, an odd pair of credentials for a picture this bloody.

A policeman gives his life to catching one man, and the chase costs him as much as it costs the man he is chasing. Jean Valjean was imprisoned for stealing bread and has been running ever since; Javert does not stop, and the pursuit outlasts whatever either of them first intended by it. Tom Hooper takes 158 minutes to move the stage version of Hugo's novel across decades and into a student revolt in France, which is roughly the arithmetic the material demands. Singing does the work a novel gives to interior monologue, so private life is amplified and history goes past in bulk. The Golden Globe for best musical or comedy picture went to it, with a place in the National Board of Review's ten. Enormous scale, narrow interest: one man, one pursuer, one debt neither will put down.

The obstacle is money — specifically, the money Oliver Barrett IV stands to inherit if he does as his father tells him. He is at Harvard reading law, Jennifer Cavilleri is studying music, and the film pairs them early and marries them soon after, well before it is finished with them. That is the structural decision worth noting: the courtship is settled in the first stretch, so what stays under test is not whether two people love each other but what a family will spend in order to be obeyed. Arthur Hiller keeps the frame narrow across 100 minutes — two young people, one father, an arrangement of class that neither charm nor appeal will shift. The Golden Globe for best drama went to it, and the National Board of Review placed it among the year's ten.

Before she married Juan Perón, Eva Duarte acted for a living, which means a film about her opens on someone already practised at being looked at. Alan Parker's 135 minutes come from the stage musical, and the adaptation inherits the difficulty the life had: Argentina loved her and Argentina could not stand her, at the same time, while a musical is a form that prefers its audience to feel one thing at a time. The response is to treat a political career as public performance — appearances, crowds, a figure arranged to be seen from a distance. It took the Golden Globe for best musical or comedy picture and a National Board of Review top-ten place. Whether that framing is a limitation or the whole argument is the interesting part.

A con needs somebody willing to trust, and the three people here have spent their lives making that impossible for one another. The son works small and steady, a short-con man with a routine and a ceiling; his estranged mother and his new girlfriend both operate at higher stakes, and each has an angle that depends on him staying where he is. Stephen Frears shot it in 1990 at 110 minutes, and the pressure in nearly every scene comes from what the people in it decline to say out loud. It took the Independent Spirit award for best feature and a National Board of Review top-ten place. The pleasure and the discomfort are the same article: watching affection performed with the identical equipment these three use on a stranger.
